$comment: The releases this project measures itself against, and the facts that identify them.
Read by the `Reference releases are intact` step in release-dmg.yml, which fails the
build if any of these tags disappears or moves to a different commit.
GitHub-side tag protection became available when this repository was made public on
2026-08-17 — rulesets need Pro or a public repository, and it is now the latter. This
check is kept alongside rather than replaced by one: a ruleset can stop a tag being
deleted, but it does not record which commit the tag is supposed to point at, nor the
digest of the artifact that was published from it. Those are the facts a fallback point
is actually made of, and they live here.
Three references. v1.0.5 is the floor, v1.0.9 closes the 1.x line, and v2.5.7 is the
current release, published on 2026-09-13. A release cannot record itself — the commit
it names is the commit that carries it, and no file can contain its own hash — so each
entry here is added by the commit after the release it describes.
v2.5.7 replaced v2.5.6, withdrawn on 2026-09-13 — release, tag and DMG. The same
to v2.1.0 through v2.4.0
on 2026-08-30, so the 2.x line is still represented by its head alone. A reference
cannot be re-cut, so the work that follows one takes a number of its own, and keeping
the list at three means retiring the release it replaces rather than letting both
stand. What that costs is named rather than hidden: a fault introduced this week is no
longer bracketed from below by anything nearer than v1.0.9. The list is kept at three
deliberately; the next reference worth adding is the first 2.x state after this one
that is worth falling back to, and adding it is a decision rather than a consequence of
publishing.
Adding or changing any value below is a deliberate act and shows up in the diff as one.

references.why: First release of the numbering that survives; everything before it was withdrawn.
The second reference: credits the corpus authors, bounds a download that had nothing but the disk to stop it, and is the recent state to fall back to rather than the floor.

The current release and the third reference. It replaced v2.5.6, withdrawn the same day, and the number moved for the rule rather than for an obstacle: a reference release is not re-cut, so work that lands after one takes a number of its own. What it carries over v2.5.6 is one correctness defect closed and the words the program uses about the corpus. The defect: building a package named the archive path three times — headers, digest, bodies — so an archive replaced between those reads left the manifest stating a provenance the package did not have, with nothing failing and nothing warning; one open descriptor now serves both passes and the digest, and a test that swaps an impostor archive at the seam fails twice on the old code. The words: the window led with «Некорректных XML – 206» and «Полностью строгий разбор насчитывает 223», which put three different questions on one scale of strictness — it now leads with the only number that costs a reader anything (206 documents this program cannot read, the ones a conversion will not take) and says the rest in prose, naming the thirteen documents that break Namespaces in XML as the well-formed XML they are. The inventory's markup note is English, the manifest's xml note says which question each count answers, and the wire carries read/unread where it carried well_formed/not_well_formed. The documents themselves are untouched: the byte mirror hashes to 7cfcdce4…35d0 exactly as it did for v2.5.6, v2.5.5 and v2.5.4; the package as a whole hashes to 91fca734…6071, moved by the inventory's wording and one note inside manifest.json.
